newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Oil majors have global ambitions to electrify. [CORRECTED 09:37 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Oil majors have global ambitions to electrify. [CORRECTED 09:37 GMT]

text.p: Fired by soaring demand for power in developing countries, oil multinationals are getting connected to the global electricity industry.

Threatened by cut-throat competition in their usual markets and pressure to "green" the energy industry, oil companies are muscling on to the traditional turf of state utility companies in a bid to secure future profits.
Vast international companies more accustomed to prospecting for oil and gas and selling petroleum products have set up divisions to buy power generators or finance and build electricity plants.
The lure is a share in the exploding demand for electricity, principally in Asia and Latin America, where power-hungry industries are the motors of fast economic growth.
In the decade from 1995 to 2005, electricity demand in Asia will grow by 66 percent, say analysts Wood Mackenzie.
In Europe growth is predicted to be 25 percent, while less populous and less developed Latin America will need 50 percent more than it is currently producing.

By some estimates around $600 billion will have to be spent in the next 10 years to build the equivalent of 1,600 standard 600 megawatt (MW) power stations to satisfy the growing appetite for electricity.
FREE MARKETS EQUAL BIG OPENINGS
To satisfy that demand governments of both mature and emerging economies have relinquished the state monopoly of power provision and turned to private enterprise.

Oil companies are now jostling with international engineering, construction and generating companies for stakes in the independent power projects expected to provide 20 to 40 percent of new output in the next decade.
Oil giant Royal Dutch/Shell said this year it planned a major move into world electricty markets.
"There are real profits to be made for the oil companies," said Dennis Eklof, a director of research group Cambridge Energy Associates.
"It plays to their strengths in organising long-term international deals, dealing with high levels of political risk and their power to raise capital," he added.
But approaches to new opportunities vary. In some places electricity is an oil industry by-product, and its sale simply increases the efficiency of core activities.

Japanese oil firms recently won tenders to provide power to utilities after the wholesale electricity market was liberalised and have begun to build power plants to burn residual fuel oil, a refinery waste product.
Italian oil companies are spending over $3 billion to build three gasification plants, which turn refinery residues, for which the market is shrinking, into gases that are burnt to make electricity.

The plants are due on line by 2000, with a planned output of 10 billion kilowatts a year. Elsewhere oil companies burn fuel to power their petro-chemical plants and sell what surplus energy they produce.
RICHEST PICKINGS IN GAS
But by far the richest opportunities for oil companies lie in familiar fields.

With hydro-power limited by geography, coal frowned upon as an agent of global warming and nuclear energy an unpopular bogey, the oil majors have realised they control the asset that can best meet future energy demands -- gas.
Vast new reserves have been found, consumers want the cleaner fuel and technological innovations in generation have made burning gas more efficient.
The drawback for the oil majors is that much of the gas, a difficult hydrocarbon to transport, is "stranded" far from potential markets.
"Gas and power integration is being embraced because, without power generation, gas assets just don't get developed," said Jeremy Hudson, energy analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.

An oil company will invest in power plant to secure markets for its own gas, alleviate worries over falling prices in competitive energy markets and enable it to dictate the most profitable time to exploit its resource.
"There's a degree of taking control of the situation," said Hudson. "Cutting through to the end-user (of electricity) is an attractive strategy for them."
For big players like Mobil Corp power is a key means to leverage profit from under-utilised assets.

"It gets us access to new markets, particularly some of those new emerging markets that we definitely want to grow in and it allows us to grow our core business in natural gas and LNG," said Richard Guerrant, president of Mobil Power.
Mobil's electricity division is spending a $100 million a year in project seed money, said Guerrant.

Mobil has already won markets for its Middle Eastern gas by transporting it to South Korea in liquefied form, but further development of its holdings in Qatar depend on proposed power projects in Taiwan, China and Turkey.

The U.S. giant has tendered for a contract to build a 1400 MW plant at Izmir, on the southern Turkish coast, and is in talks on developing two 2400 MW plants in coastal China, at Jiangsu, near Shangai, and Shenzen in Guandong province.
All would burn Qatari liquefied natural gas.
GAS EXPLORATION FINANCE NEEDS POWER PLANTS
Mobil is also involved in power projects in Indonesia and Peru that will "rescue" gas that would otherwise have been financially unrealistic to bring to customers.
It hopes to close financing later this year on a 50/50 joint venture with Enron Corp to build a 500 MW power plant burning gas from the Medura field in East Java.
In Peru power projects are vital to the development of the vast Camisea gas fields in high jungles 300 miles (500km) east of Lima.
Mobil and Shell plan to build a 300MW gas-fired plant to help power Peru's southern mining industries, with another 300 MW of capacity to follow once Peru's electricity grid is integrated.

The development of the Camago-Malampaya field in the southwest Philippines by the Anglo-Dutch major is also power-dependent, with 3,000 MW of generation capacity the minimum required to make the project viable.
Shell wants to install combined cycle gas turbines in a never-completed nuclear plant to produce 1500 MW of the power required, while other consortia develop the remainder.
Shell has also reached agreement in principle with Namibian partners to co-develop a $500 million 750 MW power station near Oranjemund using off-shore Kudu field gas.
While oil companies have focused on "monetizing" gas resources (turning gas assets into cash) they also see power projects as a way to capture value right down the chain from production to consumer.

"We've decided you have to be a player in all areas to capture opportunities," said a spokesman for Amoco Corp, adding that his company would seek worthwhile stand-alone investments as well as outlets for its gas.

Amoco is developing power projects in Trinidad, southern Argentina and potentially in eastern Europe. In Colombia it hopes to have a gas-fired 200 MW plant on line by the year's end which will sell power into the local spot market.
And by 1999 it hopes to have built a 350 MW gas-fired plant at Great Yarmouth in Britain to sell power on a competitive basis.
SCRAMBLE INTO POWER WILL LEAVE SOME BEHIND
European oil companies have begun to follow the lead of the multi-nationals.

Norway's Statoil and Norsk Hydro have formed a joint venture company, Naturkraft, to build the country's first gas-fired power stations. Naturkraft is currently awaiting final approval from the authorities of plans for two proposed plants (correcting to make clear plants not yet built).
France's Elf Aquitaine has bought into a British generator and Spain's Repsol SA has targeted Latin America.
"For some of them its more a question of widening their horizons abroad rather than the current project value," said Salomon's Hudson.
He and other analysts warn that the diversification into power will not be successful for all companies.

"There is a risk that in the scramble to develop assets companies might not get a high enough return on capital... if the pressure on electricity prices means that the economics can't be justified," said Hudson.
"Its people with existing assets, who can integrate their interests and get some efficiencies that will come out ahead," said Cambridge Energy's Eklof.
